source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations (LRA)
finding: Latent Relational Analysis (LRA) scores relational similarity of word pairs from corpus text patterns plus SVD, and matches the average college applicant on SAT analogies.
numbers: 374 SAT analogy questions: LRA 210 correct, 160 wrong, 4 skipped; recall 56.1%, precision 56.8%, F 56.5%. Human average 57%. 95% CI for LRA recall 51.0-61.2 (human level inside it). Random 20%. Run time almost 9 days of CPU.
quote: LRA achieves 56% on the 374 analogy questions, statistically equivalent to the average human score of 57%.
limits: Heavy compute (about 209 CPU hours, a 16-CPU cluster for one step). Needs a huge corpus (about 5x10^10 words). Human 57% is an estimate from SAT norms and may be slightly high.
agent_relevance: Relational similarity from text statistics can reach average-human level with no training, but it is an offline, costly pipeline, not a cheap online call.

source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations: LRA vs VSM and corpus size
finding: LRA beats the plain vector space model (VSM) even when VSM uses a corpus ten times larger.
numbers: SAT recall: VSM-AV (AltaVista, about 5x10^11 words) 47.1%; VSM-WMTS (about 5x10^10 words) 38.5%; LRA 56.1% on the smaller WMTS corpus. All three pairwise recall differences significant (Fisher exact, 95%). Human-level test: both VSM variants fall below 57%, LRA does not.
quote: Although VSM-AV has a corpus ten times larger than LRA's, LRA still performs better than VSM-AV.
limits: Pair-pattern counts depend on corpus size: the same VSM falls from 47.1 to 38.5 with 10x less text.
agent_relevance: Gains come from smoothing (SVD) and synonym variants, not just more data. A cheap agent-side count vector will be weaker than LRA.

source: Turney (2006) Similarity of Semantic Relations: other measures and relation classification
finding: Word-level (attributional) similarity measures do poorly on SAT analogies. LRA also classifies noun-modifier relations best.
numbers: SAT F scores: Hirst-St-Onge 33.4, Jiang-Conrath 28.5, Leacock-Chodorow 32.0, Lin 29.1, Resnik 34.4, Turney 2001 35.0, VSM 47.4, random 20.0. Noun-modifier classification (600 pairs, nearest neighbour): LRA 30 classes 39.8% (239/600), 5 classes 58.0% (348/600); VSM-AV 5-class 43.3% (260/600).
limits: Small dataset (600 pairs, about 20 per class). The paper says accuracy may not yet suit applications.
agent_relevance: Word similarity (lexicon or attributional) is not a substitute for relational similarity. Retrieval by 'same relation' needs relation-aware features.

source: Turney (2005) Measuring Semantic Similarity by Latent Relational Analysis (IJCAI-05)
finding: First report of LRA. Three changes over VSM: automatic patterns from the corpus, SVD smoothing, synonym reformulation of word pairs.
numbers: SAT 374 questions: LRA 56.4%. Noun-modifier 600 pairs, 30 classes F: VSM-AV 27.9, VSM-WMTS 24.0, LRA 35.9; 5 classes F: 43.4, 40.2, 53.6.
quote: LRA achieves state-of-the-art results, reaching human-level performance on the analogy questions
limits: Same corpus and compute limits as the 2006 journal version. Parameters were swept on the same test set.
agent_relevance: Risk of tuning on the test set applies: the 2006 sweep spans about 54-58% on SAT.

source: Turney (2006) LRA parameter sensitivity
finding: LRA results on SAT move by a few points with settings, so the 56% headline is not a sharp number.
limits: Gaps of 1-3 points on 374 questions are within sampling noise (95% CI width about 10 points).
agent_relevance: Do not read small differences between cheap similarity variants as real on a test this size.

source: Turney and Littman (2005) Corpus-based Learning of Analogies and Semantic Relations
finding: The VSM for relational similarity: build vectors of joining-phrase counts from AltaVista hit counts for each word pair, compare by cosine.
numbers: SAT: 176 of 374 correct, precision 47.7%, recall 47.1%, F 47.4%. Corpus about 10^11 words (350 million web pages at the time).
limits: Needed many search-engine queries per word pair; hit counts are unstable and the engine is gone.
agent_relevance: Direct ancestor of 'a count vector of relation types': 47% against 20% chance with no training.

source: Turney and Littman (2003) Combining Independent Modules to Solve Synonym and Analogy Problems
finding: Mixing several weak modules by a probabilistic rule beats any single one on synonym questions. Introduces the 374-item SAT analogy set.
numbers: TOEFL 80 synonym questions: LSA alone 43.8%; PMI-IR 69.0%; Thesaurus 69.6%; Connector 64.2%; all-module mixture 80.2%; logarithmic combination 82.0%; product rule 80.0%.
limits: Synonym task, not analogy; gain comes from complementary error patterns of the modules.
agent_relevance: Ensembling cheap similarity signals gave about +10 points; a model for mixing embedding similarity with LLM judgement.

source: Turney (2013) Distributional Semantics Beyond Words: SuperSim
finding: Supervised learning of the function that combines word-level similarities beats hand-coded combinations for word pairs.
numbers: SAT: SuperSim 54.8% (205/374), below LRA 56.1% and human 57%; earlier: Know-Best 43.0, k-means 44.0, BagPack 44.1, VSM 47.1, Dual-Space 51.1, BMI 51.1, PairClass 52.1, PERT 53.5. Ten-choice SAT: SuperSim 52.7 vs Dual-Space 47.9. SemEval-2012 Task 2 Spearman: SuperSim 0.408; Zhila 0.353; UTD-LDA 0.334; RNN-1600 0.275. SuperSim trains in minutes vs 9 days for LRA.
limits: Needs labelled quadruples (extra positives built by symmetry from the SAT items; 10-fold cross-validation).
agent_relevance: Relational similarity can be learned in minutes from word-pair features; supports a small learned scorer.

source: Linzen (2016) Issues in evaluating semantic spaces using word analogies
finding: The vector-offset method (argmax cos(x, a*-a+b)) partly measures neighbourhood, not relation consistency. Simple baselines do well.
numbers: If query words are not excluded the nearest neighbour of a*-a+b was b in 93% of cases and a in 5% (never a*). Reversing the analogy direction lowered accuracy by 0.11 on average over categories. Currencies category accuracy about 0.12.
quote: The method's reliance on cosine similarity conflates offset consistency with largely irrelevant neighbourhood structure
limits: word2vec/GloVe-era models and Google/BATS-style data.
agent_relevance: If an agent uses embedding offsets for 'same relation', compare with an ONLY-B baseline first and exclude query terms.

source: Nissim, van Noord, van der Goot (2020) Fair is Better than Sensational: Man is to Doctor as Woman is to Doctor
finding: The famous 'man is to doctor as woman is to nurse' bias analogies are partly an artefact: the standard code forbids returning any input word.
numbers: Unconstrained 3CosAdd/3CosMul returns B (doctor) for man:doctor::woman:X. Bolukbasi's method used a 50,000-word cutoff that removed gynecologist (rank 51,839) and computer_programmer (57,255). Tables 1-2 compare constrained vs unconstrained accuracy on the Google analogy set.
limits: Argument rests on a few examples plus accuracy tables; it does not show that no bias exists.
agent_relevance: Analogy-by-offset output depends on hidden implementation constraints; do not over-read it.

source: Ethayarajh, Duvenaud, Hirst (2019) Towards Understanding Linear Word Analogies
finding: Proves when vector arithmetic solves analogies for SGNS/GloVe: a linear analogy holds iff co-occurrence shifted PMI (csPMI) is equal across pairs and the words are contextually coplanar.
numbers: Theorem needs exact reconstruction of the word-context matrix; squared Euclidean distance is a decreasing linear function of csPMI. Experiments support the assumptions under noise.
quote: a linear analogy holds over a set of ordered word pairs iff csPMI(x, y) is the same for every word pair
limits: Static SGNS/GloVe only, not transformers.
agent_relevance: Says when cheap vector arithmetic is justified: the relation must show as a stable co-occurrence shift.

source: Chen, Peterson, Griffiths (2017) Evaluating vector-space models of analogy
finding: The parallelogram model on word2vec/GloVe predicts human relational similarity ratings unevenly across relation types, and human ratings violate geometry.
numbers: Exp 1: 823 MTurk participants (158 excluded), SemEval-2012 pairs; mean rating 4.52; within-subtype 5.01, between-subtype 4.02, between-type 2.70. Cosine fails on SIMILAR, CONTRAST, NON-ATTRIBUTE; best on CASE RELATIONS; Euclidean best on SPACE-TIME. Exp 2: 1,102 participants (99 excluded), ratings asymmetric by presentation order. Exp 3: 71 participants (11 excluded), triangle inequality broken; expected pattern in 7 of 12 triads.
limits: MTurk samples, English, static embeddings.
agent_relevance: Human relational similarity is asymmetric and context-dependent, so one fixed cosine misses cases; keep the cheap score as a candidate filter only.

source: Brown et al. (2020) Language Models are Few-Shot Learners: SAT analogies
finding: GPT-3 175B solves SAT analogies at or above the average college applicant, and improves with in-context examples and scale.
numbers: 374 SAT questions: zero-shot 53.7%, one-shot 59.1%, few-shot 65.2%; average applicants 57%; random 20%. 175B vs 13B: more than 10 points better.
quote: On this task GPT-3 achieves 65.2% in the few-shot setting, 59.1% in the one-shot setting, and 53.7% in the zero-shot setting
limits: Possible contamination of the public SAT set is not ruled out in the task text.
agent_relevance: A plain LLM few-shot beats the 2006 text-statistics system (LRA 56.1) by 9 points; text statistics is no longer the best scorer, only a cheap one.

source: Ushio et al. (2021) BERT is to NLP what AlexNet is to CV: Can PLMs identify analogies?
finding: Pretrained LMs scored zero-shot on word analogy multiple-choice questions barely beat LRA and static embeddings, and are very sensitive to template and scoring choices.
numbers: Full SAT 374: LRA 56.4; GPT-3 zero-shot 53.7, few-shot 65.2 (uses training examples); best LMs tuned on full SAT land in the same mid-50s range (table partly garbled in text extraction). Google set: FastText about 96.6, close to or above LMs. Masking head or tail of answer words still leaves above-chance scores (e.g. RoBERTa Google head 60.6, tail 55.8), an answer-similarity shortcut. Permutations mixing the two pairs (a:c::b:d) hurt most.
quote: even with optimal hyperparameter values, LMs barely outperform the performance of the simpler LRA model
limits: Best template, scoring function and weights vary by dataset. Harder-for-human items are also harder for models.
agent_relevance: Keep the a:b::c:d order in prompts. Datasets have a similarity shortcut, so strong benchmark scores may not mean relation reasoning.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matches or beats UCLA undergraduates on text matrices, letter strings, and four-term verbal analogies, but is weaker on far story analogies.
numbers: Digit matrices (N=40): GPT-3 above humans, OR 1.88 (p=0.005) generation, OR 6.27 multiple choice. Letter strings N=57: OR 1.76 on zero-generalization. Verbal analogies: as good or better than humans on UCLA VAT (N=57) and Sternberg-Nigro, above estimated SAT average on 374 SAT items; numerically weaker on Jones et al. with the same semantic-distance cost (OR 3.24, p=0.0165). Story analogies (N=54): humans better, OR 0.37 (p=0.0003); GPT-3 far-analogy p=0.065; 15 of 54 humans always chose the analogous story.
limits: Nature Human Behaviour 2023. One model, temperature 0. Contamination argued against but not excluded.
agent_relevance: Lexical-relation analogies are within LLM reach; cross-domain structural analogies are the weak spot, where an explicit mapping step is most needed.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Re-testing Webb et al. letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets, LLMs drop sharply while humans do not.
numbers: Prolific humans N=136. Accuracy across all alphabets and problem types: humans 0.753 [0.734, 0.773] (1,876 samples), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Humans barely dropped from standard to permuted alphabets; GPT models dropped, then dropped again for symbol alphabets. On the original problems GPT scored below humans, unlike in Webb et al.
quote: these models lack the robustness and generality of human analogy-making
limits: Letter-string domain, zero-generalization setting, temperature 0. The Hodel-West prompt format worked best.
agent_relevance: Emergent-analogy claims rest on familiar content. A scaffold should test an analogy on a transformed instance before trusting it.

source: Czinczoll et al. (2022) Scientific and Creative Analogies in Pretrained Language Models (SCAN)
finding: On analogies across distant domains (SCAN), BERT, GPT-2 and GloVe all score very low, unlike on the easier BATS set.
numbers: Mean reciprocal rank on BATS: GloVe .099, GPT-2 .098, BERT .207, M-BERT .205. On SCAN: GloVe .022, GPT-2 .057, BERT .044, M-BERT .041. Metaphor subset: GloVe .006, GPT-2 .054.
limits: Small LMs (GPT-2, BERT-base), not instruction-tuned. A worked example and fine-tuning change scores.
agent_relevance: Static similarity and small-LM scoring both fail for far analogies, in line with using cheap similarity only for near retrieval.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) ANALOGYKB: a million-scale analogy knowledge base
finding: A knowledge base of analogies built from ConceptNet and Wikidata improves analogy recognition for small LMs and analogy generation for LLMs.
numbers: About 63% of unfiltered sampled data points did not form real analogies. RoBERTa-Large trained on 10,000 ANALOGYKB points improved on E-KAR, BATS, UNIT 2, UNIT 4, Google and SAT; training on unchecked data lowered performance; sentence embeddings did worse than word-embedding differences.
limits: Exact table values not copied here; text states gains and 'rivaling human performance on some tasks'.
agent_relevance: Quality of relation pairs matters more than quantity: 63% noise hurt results.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-Context Analogical Reasoning with Pre-Trained Language Models
finding: Turning visual Raven-matrix features into words lets a text LM solve them zero-shot; how the problem is put into words matters a lot.
numbers: GPT-3 175B on Center: 77.2% with attribute naming, 80.0% with decomposition (+2.8). OPT-125M rose from 22.2% to 45.6% with decomposition. 2x2Grid up to 78.0%, 3x3Grid 86.4%. Controls: 72.6% and 77.8% with random values vs 76.0% and 80.0% with RAVEN values. Chance 12.5%.
limits: Human reference came from a task-trained setting, so the comparison is loose.
agent_relevance: Verbalisation (naming, then decomposing) changed accuracy by tens of points for small models; representation of relations in words is a lever.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024): similarity-retrieval baseline
finding: Embedding-based retrieval of similar solved problems (Sentence-BERT cosine, top-5) is a strong baseline; self-generated exemplars beat it only for strong LLMs.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy, 5-shot retrieved CoT vs self-generated: text-davinci-003 57% vs 61%; davinci-002 47% vs 48%; davinci-001 11% vs 9%; curie-001 3% vs 2%. 0-shot CoT at davinci-003 50%. GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K: 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, ours 77.8.
quote: Our method outperforms the retrieved CoT with larger-scale LLMs
limits: Only top-5 cosine on problem text was tested, not relational features.
agent_relevance: Direct case of cheap vector-similarity retrieval inside an LLM prompt: it wins for weak models and loses slightly for strong ones.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy Generation by Prompting LLMs (InstructGPT)
finding: Prompt wording changes InstructGPT analogy quality; imperative statements at low temperature beat questions; model size matters.
numbers: Human-rated meaningful analogies on 1.4k generations; the largest InstructGPT is comparable to human references in the no-source setting; relative gains of 19.17% and 15.34% from 0.3B to 1.3B parameters; the explanation task is still below humans.
limits: One model family, one rating pool.
agent_relevance: Prompt phrasing is a measurable lever for analogy generation: use direct imperatives and low temperature.

source: Turney (2006) LRA method note: how text statistics become a relation vector
finding: LRA pipeline: find joining phrases for each word pair in a corpus, build a pair-by-pattern matrix, smooth with SVD, compare by cosine over many synonym-swapped variants.
numbers: Sparse matrix 17,232 word pairs by 8,000 patterns, 5.8% non-zero; 12 pipeline steps; synonyms from Lin's thesaurus; one SAT question needs 6 word pairs.
limits: Expensive; later SuperSim and LM scoring replaced it.
agent_relevance: A tiny version (a count vector of relation words) is feasible; full LRA is not agent-time work.

source: Turney (2006) LRA vs human SAT estimate (method of comparison)
finding: The 57% human mean is an estimate: average college-bound seniors score about 57% on verbal SAT analogy items, and the paper says this may be slightly high.
numbers: VSM-AV recall 47.1% CI 42.2-52.5 (below human); VSM-WMTS 38.5% CI 33.5-43.6 (below); LRA 56.1% CI 51.0-61.2 (not distinguishable from 57%).
limits: Human figure is not from a matched sample of test takers.
agent_relevance: Treat 'human-level' claims as 'inside a wide interval', not a win.

source: Ushio et al. (2021) BERT is to NLP what AlexNet is to CV: difficulty levels
finding: Items that are harder for humans (U2, U4 educational sets) are also harder for LMs; hard items are abstract or use rare words.
numbers: Example hard items: witness:testimony::generator:electricity (abstract) and grouch:cantankerous::palace:ornate (rare words). Figure 4 shows accuracy falling with level in U2 and U4.
limits: Number of answer candidates varies 3-5 across U2/U4, so per-level scores are not fully comparable.
agent_relevance: Text-statistics similarity fails where relation words are rare or abstract; route such cases to explicit reasoning.

source: Turney and Littman (2005) VSM: why word-level similarity fails
finding: Relational similarity is measured on word pairs via pair-pattern vectors, not by combining word similarities, which gets only about 35% on SAT analogies.
numbers: Word-similarity based best baselines on SAT: Turney 2001 35.0 F, Resnik 34.4 F vs VSM 47.4 F (random 20.0), from the 2006 comparison table.
limits: Comparison table appears in the 2006 paper; VSM figures from the 2005 paper.
agent_relevance: For retrieval of analogues, compare relations (pair-level features), not just topic words.
